value.ESI1: 1 physician, 2 nurses, 1 EMT; blood, X-ray, CT (70% modeled)
value.ESI2: 1 physician, 2 nurses, 1 EMT; blood, X-ray, CT (70% modeled)
value.ESI3: 1 physician, 1 nurse; blood, X-ray, CT (30% modeled)
value.ESI5: 1 physician assistant, 1 nurse; no listed test

data.unit: staff/test slots per simulated patient; conditional CT share (%)
data.source_evidence_basis: The authors describe an ED-specific DES built from patient severity, staff interviews, and observed workflow. Its local ESI matrix assigns different staff roles and diagnostics by acuity; ESI 1–2 have physician, nurse, EMT and blood/X-ray/CT requirements, whereas ESI 4–5 route to a PA with a nurse and less testing.
data.limitations: This is one site’s model specification, not measured universal protocol or observed simultaneous concurrency. Authors assume equipment is fully operational and staff available without breaks; local staffing and diagnostic protocols may differ.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use acuity as a routing/priority attribute and configure role/equipment bundles as explicit scenario parameters. Do not use percentages or slots as RWJ facts.

value.revisit: ESI 1–4 receive second nurse and physician/PA visit in this model

data.unit: ordered workflow states and result-ready gate
data.source_evidence_basis: The study’s process description states patients are first seen by a nurse, then a doctor orders tests, and after tests/results are ready a physician performs a final diagnostic visit. It says nurses and clinicians are used mostly twice depending on criticality; Table 2 assigns first and second visits.
data.limitations: This is the model’s chosen workflow for one ED. The paper assumes continuously available staff and fully operational diagnostic equipment; it does not validate a universal sequence for all presentations.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Represent separate clinician encounters and a result-ready condition before final interpretation/disposition; permit clinically specified alternate branches.

value.priority_attribute: ED-specific ESI acuity/resource category, levels 1 (most urgent) through 5 (least urgent)
value.routing: ESI3 physician; ESI4-5 PA in this model

data.unit: ordinal acuity categories and role routing
data.source_evidence_basis: In the studied ED, nurses assigned ESI levels 1–5, with level 1 most urgent and level 5 least urgent. The model routes level 3 patients to physicians and levels 4–5 to physician assistants and assigns different expected resources by level.
data.limitations: This is one ED’s implementation, not a universal priority queue discipline, and the paper does not establish exact preemption behavior.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use acuity as an explicit selection attribute for the synthetic encounter queue; make tie-breaking and interruption/preemption separate configurable rules rather than implying the source prescribes them.

data.locator: Section 3.1, process description and modeled ED assets
data.source_setting: One US metropolitan ED, open 24 hours; shares diagnostics and pharmacy with hospital
data.quantity: Reported treatment-room pool and shared diagnostic assets
data.source_evidence_basis: The paper describes a 27-room ED, including two rooms equipped for CPR, two for inmates, and one for psychological patients, with X-ray, laboratory, and pharmacy shared with the hospital. These are setting characteristics stated in the source, distinct from its staffing allocation experiments.
data.limitations: A single-site paper’s inventory description; not current RWJ inventory, staffing, live availability, or proof all rooms are suitable for a specific synthetic case.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use room types and shared diagnostics as candidate resource categories in an external scenario configuration. Never transfer the counts to RWJ or interpret them as available capacity.
